## The really BIG question
<hr>
<br/>

<div align="center">**How do biological systems respond to human impacts on planet Earth?**</div>

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:240px; LEFT:200px; WIDTH:700px; HEIGHT:400px" SRC="images/connect.jpg">

## Species *Range* changes
<hr>

**<span style="color:green">Geographic range</span>= total spatial area in which a species can exist**

<br/>

<div style="float: left; width: 50%;">

**Range changes can be facilitated by individuals themselves moving**

<br/>

**For example: individuals following food resources, altering migratory pathways, etc.**

<br/>

**Can occur (1) naturally (competition) or (2) via move response or (3) changes in survival rate**

<br/>

**Changes impact a <span style="color:green">species' distribution</span> = where individuals are actually found at a given time**

</div>

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:240px; LEFT:575px; WIDTH:500px; HEIGHT:400px" SRC="images/birdsmigrate.jpg">

## Confronted with a changing world: organisms can *move*
<hr>
<br/>

**<span style="color:blue">Move</span>: movement of individuals (dispersal, migration), populations or species (range changes).**

<br/>

**What are the reasons for an organism to move?**

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:320px; LEFT:225px; WIDTH:6; HEIGHT:350px" SRC="images/arrow.jpg">

## Broad move trends: Poleward, upslope, deeper
<hr>
**With climate warming, species are moving to higher latitudes, higher elevation, and deeper (aquatic)**
<br/>
*Not every species is on the move, showing the complexity and importance of other factors*

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:240px; LEFT:100px; WIDTH:900px; HEIGHT:450px" SRC="images/shifts.png">

## Bird species in the Appalachian mtns (Deluca & King, 2017)
<hr>

- **9 out of 16 low-elevation species in the White Mountains of New Hampshire moved upslope by an average of 99 meters over a study period from 1993 to 2009**

<br/>

<div style="float: left; width: 55%;">

- **Only one high elevation species, Magnolia Warbler, exhibited evidence of an upslope shift**
    + WHY?
 
 <br/>
 
- **Several of the high elevation species shifted ranges downslope**
    + HUH?

<br/>

- **What other species/community level factors could be at play??**

</div>

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:300px; LEFT:660px; WIDTH:400px; HEIGHT:300px" SRC="images/bird3.jpg">

## Tree species in the Appalachian mtns (Deluca & King, 2017)
<hr>
<br/>

- **Northwestward Shift: Scarlet oak is appearing more frequently in areas northwest of the Appalachians.**

<br/>

<div style="float: left; width: 55%;">

- **Decrease in Southeast: a decrease in its presence in the Southeast, a region experiencing drier conditions**

<br/>

- **Studies indicate a substantial shift of over 100 miles to the northwest from the Appalachians over 30 years**

<br/>

- **Natural colonization of these northern areas might be limited within a 100-year timeframe**
    + what limits tree movement?

</div>

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:240px; LEFT:660px; WIDTH:300px; HEIGHT:400px" SRC="images/scarlet.png">

## Constraints to movement trends...
<hr>
<br/>

- **Brook trout are highly adapted to cold, oxygen-rich streams**
    + high sensitivity to small thermal changes

<div style="float: left; width: 50%;">

<br/>

- **Warming temperatures reduce habitat suitability**
<br/>
- **Drought lowers flows, which also makes water warmer**

<br/>

- **High-elevation populations in the Southern Appalachians are particularly vulnerable**
    + *climate pinching* at southern edge and upward elevation limit
    + brook trout are unable to disperse long distances

</div>

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:250px; LEFT:550px; WIDTH:550px; HEIGHT:400px" SRC="images/trout.png">

## Constraints to movement trends...
<hr>
<br/>

- **Range migration of hardwood trees (scarlet maple) is at the expense of conifer forests**

<br/>

<div style="float: left; width: 60%;">

- **Northern flying squirrel depends on mature red spruce forests**
    + thus, climate and logging threaten reduce their habitat

<br/>

- **Southern flying squirrel ranges are expanding**
    + survive in mix forests and eat nuts (hardwood)
    + carry a parasite that is lethal to Northern flying squirrel

<br/>

- **Community interdependence matters!**

</div>

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:240px; LEFT:670px; WIDTH:350px; HEIGHT:450px" SRC="images/squirrel.jpg">

## Constraints to movement trends...
<hr>
<br/>

<div style="float: left; width: 60%;">

- **High elevation Appalachian mountain tops are 'sky islands**
    + glacial relic endemic species adapted to cold

<br/>

- **Elevation limits reduce total available habitat and increase competition as other species move upslope**

<br/>

- **Mountaintop endemics like the Appalachian grizzled skipper face extinction from competition** 

<br/>

- **Fraser fir forests shrinking due to loss of cool temperatures and increased stress from invasive insects (balsam woolly adelgid)**

</div>

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:220px; LEFT:690px; WIDTH:350px; HEIGHT:450px" SRC="images/moth.jpg">

## Appalachian Mountains as a Migratory Corridor
<hr>

- **Appalachian range provides a continuous forested pathway, rich in food and shelter**
    + 'green highway' for migration (N-S) for birds, insects and mammals
 
<br/>
 
**Wood Thrush migrates from Central America to Appalachia to breed**
<br/>
**Monarch Butterfly uses the Appalachians during its long-distance migration**
<br/>
**Eastern Red Bat migrates along forested ridgelines**
<br/>
**Black-throated Green Warbler  depends on high-elevation spruce-fir forests as stop-overs**    
  
<br/>

- **Habitat fragmentation (e.g., roadways, development) disrupts continuous forest cover**

<br/>

- **Climate-driven phenological mismatch – food resources (insects, berries) peak earlier, out of sync with arrival times**

<br/>

- **Invasive species like garlic mustard reduce the quality of understory stopover habitat**

## In order to persist, species range changes are predictable
<hr>

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:160px; LEFT:125px; WIDTH:850px; HEIGHT:500px" SRC="images/movementrate.jpg">

## The 'Move Response' is limited
<hr>
<br/>

**<span style="color:blue">Move</span>: movement of individuals (dispersal, migration), populations or species (range changes).**

<br/>

**<span style="color:red">Dispersal</span>: movement away from natal territory (typically before or during reproduction - can be gametes not individuals)**

<br/>

**Dispersal is a key trait that influences move response. Can be short or long distance -  All species (even sessile ones) can disperse, but species differ in their dispersal ability.**

<br/>

**Dispersal links/limits individual movement with range shifts**

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:420px; LEFT:800px; WIDTH:200px; HEIGHT:250px" SRC="images/dispersal.jpg">

## Range changes are usually slow
<hr>

* **Many species are limited in a move response by gamete dispersal**
    + Appalachian understory plants have limited seed dispersal
    
<br/>

* **Trees are excellent disperses across many generations, however..TIME MATTERS**


<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:320px; LEFT:200px; WIDTH:650px; HEIGHT:350px" SRC="images/tree.jpg">

## Factors that influence the move response
<hr>

**Whether species can “move” as a response to global change stressors depends on many things…**

<br/>

- **<span style="color:green">Organismal traits</span>: Ability to move in response to changing conditions can be affected by many intrinsic traits like dispersal ability, generation time, etc.**
    + Appalachian salamanders are highly site-faithful
    
<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:360px; LEFT:50px; WIDTH:1000px; HEIGHT:300px" SRC="images/animalmove.png">

## Factors that influence the move response
<hr>

**Whether species can “move” as a response to global change stressors depends on many things…**

<br/>

**<span style="color:green">Landscape features</span>: Ability to move in response to changing conditions can be affected by many *characteristics of the environment* like habitat matrix (connectedness)**

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:360px; LEFT:50px; WIDTH:1000px; HEIGHT:300px" SRC="images/landscape.png">

## Factors that influence the move response
<hr>

**Whether species can “move” as a response to global change stressors depends on many things…**

<br/>

- **<span style="color:green">Dynamics of change</span>: Ability to move in response to changing conditions can be affected by many *global change stressors* like pace of change. Can they keep up?**
    + Appalachian mollusks have low vagility, can they ever move fast/far enough?

## Factors that influence the move response
<hr>

**Whether species can “move” as a response to global change stressors depends on many things…**

<br/>

**<span style="color:green">Globalization</span>: Our transport systems change prior constraints on organismal movement for some species, which can lead to biotic homogenization**
